questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Define the labor force in a chef's recipe costing context
questions.stem: In a chef's recipe costing sheet, which workers count toward the labor force when estimating production capacity?

options.text: Employed chefs plus unemployed chefs actively seeking kitchen work
Only the chefs currently cooking on the line during the dinner service
options.misconception: confuses employed with the whole labor force

options.text: Every adult in the household including retirees and students
options.misconception: includes people outside the labor force

options.text: Only the chefs paid by the hour rather than salaried staff
options.misconception: confuses pay structure with labor-force status

questions.explanation: The labor force includes both employed and unemployed individuals actively seeking work. Retirees and students not seeking work fall outside it, so counting everyone overstates it.
questions.hint: Count employed plus job-seeking unemployed only.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Compute the unemployment rate from a chef's staffing ledger
questions.stem: A chef's kitchen employs 80 cooks and has 20 unemployed cooks seeking work; what is the unemployment rate in percent?
questions.explanation: Unemployment rate equals unemployed divided by labor force times 100. With 20 unemployed and 100 in the labor force, the rate is 20 percent.
questions.hint: Divide unemployed by total labor force.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain labor force participation in a chef's payroll review
questions.stem: A chef notes that more cooks are leaving the workforce to study; explain how this affects the labor force participation rate.

answer.exemplar: The labor force participation rate falls because the number of people working or seeking work shrinks relative to the adult population, even if unemployment stays flat.

questions.explanation: Participation measures the share of adults in the labor force. When workers exit to study, that share declines, lowering participation without necessarily changing unemployment.
questions.hint: Compare labor force size to adult population.

Chefs paid above the minimum wage for their station
options.misconception: confuses pay level with employment status

options.text: Trainees who gave up searching and are no longer counted
Staff scheduled for fewer hours than they desire

questions.explanation: Hidden unemployment includes discouraged workers who stopped looking and thus are not counted in official unemployment. Overtime workers and high-paid staff do not fit this definition.
questions.hint: Look for those who stopped searching.

options.misconception: confuses recurring season with matching delay

options.text: Structural unemployment from obsolete culinary skills
options.misconception: confuses skill mismatch with search time

options.text: Cyclical unemployment from a recession in dining
options.misconception: confuses business cycle with job transitions

options.text: Frictional unemployment from job search and matching delays

questions.explanation: Frictional unemployment arises from the time needed to match workers with jobs. It is short-term and occurs even in healthy labor markets, unlike structural or cyclical types.

options.text: Structural unemployment from a skills and technology mismatch

options.misconception: confuses menu cycles with skill obsolescence

questions.explanation: Structural unemployment results from a mismatch between worker skills and job requirements, often driven by technology. Retraining is the remedy, not just waiting for demand.

questions.explanation: Cyclical unemployment rises when aggregate demand falls during a recession. It reverses when demand recovers, unlike structural unemployment.

Zero inflation at full employment

answer.exemplar: Higher expected inflation shifts the short-run Phillips curve upward, so any unemployment rate now pairs with higher actual inflation.

questions.explanation: Expected inflation enters the Phillips curve as a vertical shift. When expectations rise, the whole curve moves up, requiring higher unemployment to hold inflation steady.

questions.learningObjective: Analyze labor force changes in a chef's census
questions.stem: A chef's census shows rising population but flat labor force; what most likely explains this?

options.text: Higher inflation pushing workers out
Faster job creation absorbing all new adults
options.misconception: would raise labor force, not flatten it

options.text: Lower wages attracting more workers
More adults retiring or studying, reducing participation

questions.explanation: A flat labor force despite population growth means fewer adults participate, likely due to retirement, schooling, or discouragement.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain unemployment rate movements in a chef's economy
questions.stem: A chef observes falling unemployment alongside falling participation; explain the ambiguity.

answer.exemplar: Falling participation can lower unemployment mechanically if discouraged workers exit, masking weak labor demand.

questions.explanation: When workers stop seeking jobs, they leave the labor force, reducing both unemployment and participation. Headline improvement may hide weakness.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Identify participation drivers in a chef's survey
questions.stem: In a chef's survey, which factor would most likely raise labor force participation?

options.text: Stricter entry requirements for kitchens
A recession reducing job openings
Higher wages attracting more workers into the labor force
Longer schooling keeping youths out

questions.explanation: Higher wages incentivize more adults to enter or remain in the labor force, raising participation. Recessions and schooling tend to lower it.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish frictional from structural in a chef's hiring
questions.stem: A chef's cooks quit to find better-paying stations and take three weeks to match; this is which unemployment?

options.text: Seasonal unemployment from menu changes
Structural unemployment from obsolete skills
options.misconception: confuses search time with skill gap

options.text: Cyclical unemployment from weak demand
Frictional unemployment from job search and matching

questions.explanation: Short search time between jobs is frictional unemployment. It reflects matching delays, not skill obsolescence or demand shortfalls.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Propose a remedy for structural unemployment in a chef's kitchen
questions.stem: A chef's older cooks lack automation skills; which policy best addresses the resulting unemployment?

options.text: Lower interest rates encouraging borrowing
Demand stimulus boosting dining out
Retraining programs updating cook skills
Shorter unemployment benefits
options.misconception: may raise search but not skills

questions.explanation: Structural unemployment requires retraining or skill acquisition. Demand stimulus helps cyclical unemployment but not skill mismatches.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain cyclical unemployment policy in a chef's economy
questions.stem: A chef's economy is in recession; explain which unemployment type rises and which policy helps.

answer.exemplar: Cyclical unemployment rises during recession, and demand stimulus such as spending or rate cuts helps reduce it.

questions.explanation: Cyclical unemployment tracks the business cycle. Expansionary fiscal or monetary policy boosts demand and cuts cyclical joblessness.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish seasonal from cyclical in a chef's data
questions.stem: A chef's January layoffs repeat every year; which feature distinguishes this from cyclical unemployment?

options.text: The layoffs raise the natural rate permanently
options.misconception: seasonal does not raise natural rate

options.text: The layoffs track the business cycle peak
The layoffs affect only entry-level cooks
The layoffs recur predictably each calendar year

questions.explanation: Seasonal unemployment recurs predictably by calendar. Cyclical unemployment varies with the business cycle, not the calendar.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain Okun's law in a chef's economy
questions.stem: A chef's output falls below trend; explain what Okun's law predicts about unemployment.

answer.exemplar: Okun's law predicts unemployment rises as output falls below trend, linking the output gap to joblessness.

questions.explanation: Okun's law relates the output gap to unemployment. Below-trend output implies higher unemployment than the natural rate.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate full employment claims in a chef's economy
questions.stem: A chef claims zero unemployment is achievable; which statement best evaluates this claim?

options.text: Zero unemployment requires banning job changes
Zero unemployment is possible with enough demand stimulus
Zero unemployment is impossible due to frictional and structural
Zero unemployment only needs flexible wages

questions.explanation: Even at full employment, frictional and structural unemployment remain, so the natural rate is above zero. Demand stimulus cannot eliminate them.
